issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence only when the evidence already on record reveals a lacuna or defect that prevents it from pronouncing judgment.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to introduce settlement-register entries for the first time in the appeal to show that a third son had relinquished his share in the disputed property.
The appellate judge allowed the evidence before hearing the appeal and without first finding that the existing evidence disclosed a gap that prevented a judgment.
The existing record was sufficient for the appellate court to decide the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The additional evidence was improperly admitted and had to be ignored when deciding the case.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code gives the appellate court judicial discretion, limited to the circumstances specified in the rule. The legitimate occasion for additional evidence is an inherent lacuna or defect apparent on examining the existing evidence, not discovery of fresh evidence outside court. The test is whether the appellate court can pronounce judgment on the existing materials without the proposed evidence. The Court relied on Kessowji Issur v. G. I. P. Railway (34 I.A. 115) and Parsotim v. Lal Mohan (58 I.A. 254).

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal in which a party seeks to introduce evidence not on the trial record.
predicates.existing_record_permits_judgment: The appellate court can decide the appeal on the evidence already before it.
predicates.additional_evidence_is_newly_sought: A party seeks to introduce fresh evidence discovered outside court rather than evidence needed to fill a gap apparent in the existing record.

issues.definition: When an appeal can be decided on its existing record, a request to introduce fresh evidence discovered outside court does not permit that evidence to be admitted.

issues.legal_issue: A factual finding in a second appeal is not conclusive when it rests on improperly admitted additional evidence and ignores serious defects in that evidence.
material_facts: The first appellate court relied on additional register entries to find that the disputed property was ancestral.
Those entries had been admitted without the required basis for receiving additional evidence.
The first appellate court did not address apparent defects suggesting that the entries were interpolated or otherwise not genuine.
After excluding the additional evidence, the record did not establish that the common ancestor had owned the property or that it had passed by inheritance.
issues.conclusion: The finding based on the additional evidence could not be treated as conclusive in second appeal, and the additional evidence had to be left out of account.
issues.legal_principle: Although a finding of fact, however erroneous, ordinarily cannot be challenged in second appeal under section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code, a finding based on additional evidence that ought not to have been admitted, and reached without considering the evidence's intrinsic and palpable defects, is not conclusive. The principles governing admission of additional evidence under Order XLI, rule 27 also apply.

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is a second appeal challenging a factual finding made by the first appellate court.
predicates.factual_finding_relies_on_improperly_adm: The first appellate court's finding depends on additional evidence that should not have been admitted.
predicates.palpable_evidence_defects_were_not_consi: The first appellate court did not address serious apparent defects bearing on the evidence's genuineness.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, a factual finding is not conclusive if it depends on improperly admitted evidence whose serious apparent defects were not considered.

issues.legal_issue: An alienation of non-ancestral immovable property cannot be contested on the ground that it is contrary to custom.
material_facts: The suit sought to invalidate a will on the basis of customary restrictions on the owner's power to alienate property.
The land in one village was admitted not to be ancestral, and the evidence did not establish that the land in the other village was ancestral once the additional evidence was excluded.
The plaintiff's challenge to the alienation relied on the alleged custom.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff could not contest the alienation of the non-ancestral property on the ground that it was contrary to custom.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Punjab Act II of 1920 provides that no person may contest an alienation of non-ancestral immovable property on the ground that the alienation is contrary to custom. The Court applied that provision to reject the customary challenge.

predicates.suit_challenges_property_alienation: A suit seeks to contest an alienation of immovable property.
predicates.property_is_non_ancestral: The property at issue is not established to be ancestral.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_custom: The challenger argues that the alienation is invalid because it is contrary to custom.

issues.definition: A suit contesting an alienation is barred when the property is non-ancestral and the challenge rests on custom.
